actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: The Red Squirrel (Sciurus vulgaris) has a large range in the Palaearctic, extending from the United Kingdom, Ireland, Spain and Portugal in the west, through continental Europe, Russia, Mongolia, and northwest and northeast China to the Pacific coast (Panteleyev 1998, Gurnell and Wauters 1999). It has been introduced into multiple areas of Russia, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Ukraine, Lithuania, and Northern Kazakhstan (Pavlov et al. 1973), and introductions in the Caribbean have also occurred (Wilson et al. 2016). In Europe, it is widespread in most areas, with the exception of the Iberian peninsula (where it is absent from the southwest) and Great Britain (where it has almost completely disappeared from the south-east). It occurs only sporadically in the Balkans, and is absent from the majority of Mediterranean islands. It is found from sea level up to 3,100 m asl in the Alps (Spitzenberger 2002).
documentation.population: Although it is described as common throughout most of its range (Gurnell and Wauters 1999), there have been well-documented population declines and range contractions in the United Kingdom, Ireland, Italy and Finland (Gurnell and Pepper 1993, Wauters et al. 1997, O'Teangana et al. 2000, Selonen et al. 2010, Turkia et al. 2017). Typical densities range from less than 0.1 to 1.5 individuals per hectare (Gurnell and Wauters 1999). However, it is sufficiently common in some parts of its range to the extent that it is considered a forestry pest owing to its habit of stripping bark and feeding on conifer buds.
documentation.habitats: The Eurasian Red Squirrel is found in coniferous forests, deciduous woods, mixed forests, parks, gardens, and small stands of conifers, from lowland to subalpine areas. Urban environments can support denser populations (Fingland et al. 2022). The Eurasian Red Squirrel nests in cavities or constructs spherical dreys from leaves, pine needles, and twigs placed high in the canopy. It is primarily herbivorous and will consume seeds, acorns, fungus, bark, and sapwood, although it occasionally takes animal prey (young birds and eggs) (Shuttleworth et al. 2015). It scatterhoards foods to provide a winter food store, aiding the reforestation process (Zhang et al. 2020). Young are born most often in February–April and May–August, with 1–6 individuals per litter (Wilson et al. 2016).
documentation.threats: In Britain and Italy the population has declined significantly following widespread habitat loss and out-competition by the introduced Grey Squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis) from North America in the 19th century (Gurnell and Pepper 1993, Wauters et al. 1997, Bertolino and Genovesi 2003). Now that the Grey Squirrel has become established on the European continent, it is possible that it may also spread through much more of the Eurasian Red Squirrel's range. Grey Squirrels can carry the “squirrelpox” virus (SQPV), which can present asymptomatically but is fatal to Eurasian Red Squirrels (Carroll et al. 2008). When the virus is present, the Grey Squirrel can replace the Eurasian Red Squirrel up to 25 times faster than the normal replacement rate (Rushton et al. 2006). Additional threats include the use of this species in the fur and pet trade Stubbe (1965), though these threats remain unquantified. In urban areas, road traffic accidents are also a notable cause of mortality (Fingland et al. 2022).
documentation.measures: It is listed on Appendix III of the Bern Convention, and it occurs in many protected areas throughout its wide range. It is listed on the Chinese Red list as Near Threatened, and on the British Red List of Mammals as Endangered (Mathews and Harrower 2020). Urban areas may be suitable refugia for the Eurasian Red Squirrel, provided good-quality greenspaces are provided and Grey Squirrel populations are managed (Fingland et al. 2022).
documentation.use_trade: This species has been used for clothing and as a pet, though limited information is available and it is not clear to what extent it may be taken from the wild/traded for these reasons. In Mongolia, unsustainable hunting for skins for the international fur trade was a known threat in the mid-1900s, though current hunting levels are unknown.
documentation.rationale: This species has a large population size and a wide distribution, with a considerable extent of occurrence of 41,804,212 km<sup>2 </sup>and it occurs in many protected areas throughout its wide range. In Britain and Italy, the population has declined significantly following widespread habitat loss and out-competition, however, such declines have not yet been observed across major areas of this species range. Therefore, it is assessed as Least Concern, but population and threat monitoring is recommended.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: This species is now recognised as distinct from Sciurus meridionalis which was previously described as a subspecies of S. vulgaris. S. meridionalis is now considered a separate species based on morphological and genetic data and is restricted to Calabria (southwestern Italy).
